title: Interpreting a 95% confidence interval for mean subscription spend
scenario_markdown: A digital streaming platform conducts a survey of $n = 250$ randomly chosen active subscribers to estimate monthly household entertainment spending. Using standard estimation methods, the platform calculates a $95\%$ confidence interval of $[\$45.20, \$52.80]$ for the population mean monthly spend $\mu$. The analytics team drafts summary talking points for the executive committee.

parameters.objective: Distinguish valid long-run capture rate from probability statements on fixed parameters

assumptions: Random sample from the target subscriber population
Sample size n = 250 is large enough for CLT guarantees

approval.notes: Reviewed conceptual items on confidence interval interpretation. Targets the central introductory statistics misconception: once calculated, a confidence interval either contains the fixed parameter mu or does not (probability is 0 or 1); 95% refers to the long-run frequency of intervals generated by repeated sampling.

stages.prompt_markdown: Which of the following statements provides the only statistically accurate interpretation of this $95\%$ confidence interval $[\$45.20, \$52.80]$?

options.text_markdown: If we took many repeated random samples of size $250$ and computed a $95\%$ confidence interval from each, approximately $95\%$ of those intervals would contain the true population mean monthly spend $\mu$.
There is a $95\%$ probability that the true population mean $\mu$ falls between $\$45.20$ and $\$52.80$.
options.hint_markdown: Under frequentist inference, the population parameter $\mu$ is a fixed constant, not a random variable. The specific interval $[45.20, 52.80]$ either contains $\mu$ or it does not; the probability is either $1$ or $0$.

options.text_markdown: $95\%$ of all individual subscribers in the population spend between $\$45.20$ and $\$52.80$ per month.
options.hint_markdown: A confidence interval for $\mu$ estimates the center (mean) of the population, not the spread containing $95\%$ of individual customer observations.

options.text_markdown: There is a $95\%$ probability that any future sample mean from a new sample of $250$ subscribers will fall between $\$45.20$ and $\$52.80$.
options.hint_markdown: A confidence interval estimates the fixed population parameter $\mu$, not the capture probability of subsequent sample statistics.

stages.explanation_markdown: The $95\%$ confidence level describes the long-run reliability of the estimation procedure: across repeated independent samples of identical size, $95\%$ of the resulting intervals will capture the fixed parameter $\mu$. It does not state that $\mu$ has a $95\%$ probability of being in this particular realized interval, nor does it describe individual customer dispersion.

stages.prompt_markdown: Why is the statement "$P(\$45.20 \le \mu \le \$52.80) = 0.95$" formally incorrect in classical frequentist statistics?

options.text_markdown: Because the population mean $\mu$ is an unknown fixed constant, not a random variable; once the numerical interval is computed, it either captures $\mu$ or fails to capture it.
Because the statement is only valid when the sample size $n$ exceeds $1{,}000$.
options.hint_markdown: The philosophical flaw has nothing to do with sample size; it stems from whether the parameter $\mu$ is treated as a random variable or a fixed constant.

options.text_markdown: Because the calculation should have used $z$ instead of $t$ for large samples.
options.hint_markdown: The $z$ vs $t$ distribution choice determines interval width, but does not alter the fundamental frequentist interpretation of confidence.

options.text_markdown: Because the Central Limit Theorem only applies to proportions, not to monetary spending amounts.
options.hint_markdown: The CLT applies directly to means of continuous quantitative variables like monetary spending.

stages.explanation_markdown: In classical frequentist statistics, parameters (like $\mu$) are fixed, unchanging values. Randomness lies in the sampling process that creates the interval endpoints $[\bar{X} - E, \bar{X} + E]$. Before data collection, $P(\bar{X} - E \le \mu \le \bar{X} + E) = 0.95$. But after numerical calculation, no randomness remains: the realized interval $[45.20, 52.80]$ either encloses $\mu$ (probability 1) or does not (probability 0).
